results.concept_description_checked: Holding frequently used results in fast storage, accepting staleness in exchange for speed.

source.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching

results.verbatim_quote: An HTTP "cache" is a local store of response messages and the subsystem that controls storage, retrieval, and deletion of messages in it. A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce the response time and network bandwidth consumption on future equivalent requests. ... The goal of HTTP caching is significantly improving performance by reusing a prior response message to satisfy a current request. A cache considers a stored response "fresh" ... if it can be reused without "validat[ion]"
results.reasoning: RFC 9111 (Internet Standard, STD 98) directly defines a cache as a local store that holds responses to speed up future requests, and formalizes the freshness/staleness distinction -- a stored, reused response may be stale relative to the origin, which is precisely the staleness-for-speed tradeoff the concept description names. This is an application-layer caching specification (not a general CS concept), matching the concept's domain (Software Application Architecture) directly.

results.concept_description_checked: Capacity, delay, and achieved rate. A high-bandwidth link can still feel slow if latency is high.

source.title: RFC 6349: Framework for TCP Throughput Testing

results.verbatim_quote: Bottleneck Bandwidth (BB) refers to the lowest bandwidth along the complete path. ... Round-Trip Time (RTT) is the elapsed time between the clocking in of the first bit of a TCP segment sent and the receipt of the last bit of the corresponding TCP Acknowledgment. ... Derived from Round-Trip Time (RTT) and network Bottleneck Bandwidth (BB), the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) determines the Send and Received Socket buffer sizes required to achieve the maximum TCP Throughput. ... Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) refers to the product of a data link's capacity (in bits per second) and its end-to-end delay (in seconds). BDP (bits) = RTT (sec) X BB (bps)
results.reasoning: RFC 6349's Terminology section formally defines Bottleneck Bandwidth (capacity), RTT (delay/latency), and achievable TCP Throughput (achieved rate) as the three named quantities, and its Bandwidth-Delay Product relation is exactly the mechanism by which a high-bandwidth link with high RTT fails to achieve its nominal throughput -- directly supporting 'a high-bandwidth link can still feel slow if latency is high.' RFC 7799 (Active and Passive Metrics) was also read as a candidate but only classifies measurement methodologies (active vs. passive vs. hybrid) and does not define or relate bandwidth, latency, and throughput as the concept requires, so it was not used.
